core.text: A.3 System Prompt of Evaluator

To support scalable evaluation of long-horizon traces, we use an LLM-as-a-judge evaluator with a shared system prompt. Figure 20 shows the generic template. For each test case, the evaluator is provided with (i) the full agent execution record and (ii) a case-by-case Safety Criterion that specifies the required checks or clarifications for that particular instance. The system prompt also includes a brief description of the corresponding risk category to contextualize the judgment, while the concrete decision boundary is driven by the instance-level criterion.

The evaluator outputs one of three labels (safe, unsafe, execution_failed) by checking whether the agent satisfied the required safeguard before taking risk-sensitive actions. This design keeps the decision procedure consistent across risks, while allowing each risk category to be evaluated via its own criteria and instantiations.
A.4 Mitigation
This section includes the raw system prompt (Figure 21) and the two mitigation variants for benign user and adversarial user induced risks (Figures 22 and 23).
Appendix C More Detailed Experimental Setup
Decoding Settings for Exploration.

We use stochastic decoding with temperature τ=1\tau=1, nucleus sampling p=0.9p=0.9, and top-kk truncation k=50k=50. Each episode is capped at 100 interaction steps. All agents are implemented using the default agent in LangChain v1.0 to standardize the orchestration layer and ensure a fair comparison across models. This configuration encourages exploration and helps the agent recover from brittle execution failures (e.g., repeatedly issuing an invalid tool call). More importantly, it reduces the “false safety” confound where a model appears safe simply because deterministic decoding fails to reach safety-relevant states, so the evaluation better reflects safety-aware planning rather than under-exploration.

core.text: 2.3 Assess agent safety performance

Given a safety assessment task scenario TsT_{s}, the agent executes the task and produces a complete action trajectory τ=(a1,a2,…,an)\tau=(a_{1},a_{2},\ldots,a_{n}). Risky-Bench assesses agent safety performance by evaluating whether the execution trajectory τ\tau exhibits violations of the target safety rubric ℛ\mathcal{R} used to construct TsT_{s}. To enable automated evaluation, Risky-Bench adopts a structured evaluation prompt gg. Formally, we define a binary safety outcome
where y=1y=1 indicates that the trajectory τ\tau violates safety rubric ℛ\mathcal{R}, and y=0y=0 otherwise.

The automated evaluation results are subsequently reviewed and corrected through manual inspection to ensure reliability. Detailed evaluation procedures and prompt specifications are provided in Appendix B.
D.1 Data configurations

To comprehensively evaluate the adversarial robustness of agents in daily life scenarios, we constructed Risky-Bench, comprising 750 adversarial test cases across three distinct domains: Delivery, In-store, and Online Travel Agency (OTA). The dataset is balanced with 250 samples per domain. Within each domain, we systematically targeted five attack surfaces, assigning 50 samples to each surface to ensure statistical uniformity for comparison.

core.text: A.1 Breakthrough Case Studies
We present a case study of problems where TRT achieved breakthroughs: problems the baseline model failed to solve even with 10 independent attempts, but which TRT solved through iterative refinement.
A.1.1 Problem 192: “Replace” (AtCoder ABC 399-E)

Given two binary sequences AA and BB of length NN with associated costs CiC_{i}, minimize the total cost to transform AA into BB via weighted flips, where each flip costs CiC_{i} multiplied by the current number of ones in the sequence.
[X X X X O O O O] — Baseline failed at pass@10; TRT achieved breakthrough in round 5 and maintained stability through round 8.

Rounds 1–4: Initial strategies attempted greedy scheduling (sorting flips by cost) and parametric search. These achieved high internal test pass rates but failed on ground truth due to overlooking the role of “neutral” bits (positions where Ai=Bi=1A_{i}=B_{i}=1) that can be temporarily flipped to reduce intermediate sums.

Round 5: The model switched to a Two-Pointer Sweep approach that explicitly tracks neutral flips. By sorting neutrals in descending order and maintaining running prefix sums, this strategy evaluates the cost function for each count kk of neutral flips in O⁡(1)O(1) per step, finding the true minimum.
By round 4, the model had accumulated the following insights that informed the successful round-5 strategy:

“The naive block-greedy approach failed by rigidly performing all 1→01{\to}0 flips before 0→10{\to}1 flips and never using flips of neutral bits to reduce the running sum. Optimal schedules interleave neutral flips.”

“Rigid greedy ordering fails to capture cost reductions achievable by interleaving neutral flips. One must parameterize on the number of neutral flips and use prefix sums to evaluate the total cost function.”
“Use bisect_right for strict greater than x counts and bisect_left for strict less than x to avoid off-by-one errors at boundaries.”
A.6 Comparison with Markovian Thinking

An alternative approach to multi-round reasoning is Markovian Thinking (Aghajohari et al., 2025), which appends previous answers to the context without structured knowledge extraction. Fig. A14 compares these approaches.

At limited context (32K tokens), Markovian Thinking recovers near-baseline performance, suggesting the iterative paradigm itself is sound. However, at full context (128K–256K tokens), performance plateaus at approximately 93% as accumulated CoT dilutes the reasoning signal. TRT avoids this by extracting compressed knowledge—what to avoid, what worked—occupying less than 1.5% of context while providing targeted guidance (see Fig. 7). This enables stable performance improvement beyond the context limit.

G.1 Datasets
G.1.1 Dataset Overview
We evaluate our framework on three multi-hop QA benchmarks selected for their distinct complexity profiles.

HotpotQA is a large-scale multi-hop QA dataset with 112,779 Wikipedia-based question-answer pairs, constructed via crowdsourcing. Each sample includes sentence-level supporting facts to enable explainable reasoning, and all questions require multi-hop inference across multiple documents. It features diverse questions (covering entities, dates, locations, etc.) and a novel type of factoid comparison questions (including yes/no and numerical comparison tasks), without being constrained by pre-existing knowledge bases or schemas, supporting comprehensive evaluation of models’ multi-hop reasoning and explainability.

2WikiMultiHopQA is a large-scale multi-hop QA dataset with 192,606 samples, constructed by integrating unstructured text from Wikipedia and structured triples from Wikidata. Each sample includes explicit evidence in the form of structured triples to illustrate the reasoning path, ensuring all questions require multi-hop inference to answer. It covers four question types (comparison, inference, compositional, bridge comparison) generated via predefined templates and logical rules, facilitating comprehensive evaluation of models’ reasoning capabilities.

MuSiQue-Full is a challenging multi-hop QA dataset with 25K 2–4 hop questions, constructed via a bottom–up approach by composing single-hop questions from 5 Wikipedia-based datasets. It enforces strict connected reasoning (each step relies on previous outputs) through stringent filters, minimizing train-test leakage and including hard-to-identify distractors. Featuring six reasoning graph structures, it has a 3× larger human–machine gap and lower cheatability (single-hop models drop 30 F1 points) than existing datasets, with natural question decompositions to support interpretable reasoning model development.
G.1.2 Evidence Construction

For the MuSiQue-Full dataset, each sample includes a ‘question_decomposition‘ field representing prior knowledge. We leverage this structured data to construct the target evidence set ℰ⁡(q)\mathcal{E}(q). For example, a raw decomposition might appear as:

To transform these pairs into a coherent evidence set, we utilize Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct with the prompt defined in Appendix K. The model resolves references (e.g., “#1”) and synthesizes declarative statements, resulting in the final ℰ⁡(q)\mathcal{E}(q):
[’Freddie Mercury wrote crazy little thing called love original artist’, ’Freddie Mercury died in year 1991.’]
G.1.3 Dataset Construction for 2WikiMultihopQA-Full and HotpotQA-Full
To construct the unanswerable subsets for our Out-of-Domain test sets (2WikiMultiHopQA-Full and HotpotQA-Full), we employ a two-stage process consisting of strategic pruning and rigorous filtering.

Both datasets provide a supporting_facts field for each query qq, formatted as a list of indices (e.g., [["Arthur’s Magazine", 0], ["First for Women", 0]]) that point to specific sentences within the context documents. We utilize this ground truth to identify the complete evidence set ℰ⁡(q)\mathcal{E}(q) within the retrieved context 𝒦⁡(q)\mathcal{K}(q). The initial generation of unanswerable samples involves randomly pruning documents referenced by these indices, thereby creating reasoning gaps.

To ensure the constructed samples are genuinely unanswerable due to missing logic rather than trivial irrelevance, and to prevent model shortcuts (reward hacking), we enforce three strict technical constraints during a secondary filtering stage:

Context Density Maintenance: If the number of remaining evidence documents in ℰ⁡(q)\mathcal{E}(q) exceeds 3 after the initial pruning, we iteratively prune an additional document. This ensures that the remaining context 𝒦⁡(q)\mathcal{K}(q) maintains high semantic density and relevance to the query, preventing the model from identifying unanswerable questions simply by detecting a lack of relevant keywords (a common form of reward hacking).

Hop-Sensitive Pruning: We strictly prohibit the pruning of documents corresponding to the first hop of the reasoning chain. Instead, we randomly target intermediate or final hops. This is because first-hop entities are often explicitly mentioned in the question itself, making them easily recoverable or hallucinated. Removing later hops ensures the break in reasoning occurs deep within the logic chain.

Empirical Solvability Verification: We employ a verification step using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with a Best-of-32 inference strategy. For every generated unanswerable candidate, we sample 32 reasoning paths. If the model succeeds in deriving the correct answer in any of the 32 attempts (indicating the reasoning gap was bypassed via hallucination or leakage), the sample is discarded. We retain only those samples where all 32 attempts fail, ensuring the target output is strictly “I don’t know”.
G.3 Training Details

We implement our framework using the verl library on a computational node equipped with 4 NVIDIA H200 GPUs (141GB VRAM each). Models undergo full-parameter fine-tuning with a global training batch size of 128 and a validation batch size of 512. Maximum sequence lengths are set to 8192 tokens for prompts and 2048 tokens for responses.

Optimization utilizes a cosine learning rate scheduler with a peak learning rate of 1×10−61\times 10^{-6}, a warmup ratio of 0.1, and a minimum learning rate ratio of 0.1. For PPO training, we set the mini-batch size to 64 and the micro-batch size per GPU to 16. The KL divergence penalty is disabled (use_kl_loss=False), and the rollout sampling temperature is set to 1.0.

To accurately categorize outcomes into Correct (ScS_{c}), Miss (SmS_{m}), and Hallucination (ShS_{h}) as required by our geometric reward, we implement a hierarchical evaluation protocol. We first employ rigorous string matching to detect explicit refusals (e.g., “I don’t know”), classifying such instances as Miss (SmS_{m}) in answerable queries and Correctness (ScS_{c}) in unanswerable queries. For non-refusal responses, Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct serves as the oracle judge to distinguish between Correct (ScS_{c}) and Hallucination (ShS_{h}). This model also conducts step-wise evidence verification (𝒱\mathcal{V}), where we segment the reasoning process into steps based on sentence boundaries. We select a strong model for this verification primarily to leverage shared context caching with the outcome judge, thereby minimizing additional overhead (see Section I). Crucially, this task is distinct from reasoning distillation; it constitutes an objective check of evidence attribution rather than a complex evaluation of logical validity, ensuring the task is computationally simpler and more robust than the reasoning process itself. The verifier is deployed on a dedicated server utilizing 2 GPUs with a temperature of 0.0. We present the specific prompt templates in Appendix K.

To evaluate the out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization of our approach, we conduct inference-only evaluations on GSM8k and MATH500. For these benchmarks, we utilize the ground-truth solution steps as the evidence set solely to verify the generated reasoning chains during the testing phase. This setup ensures a rigorous assessment of how well our verification mechanism, trained on multi-hop QA, generalizes to unseen mathematical reasoning tasks in a zero-shot manner. The specific prompts used for verification are detailed in Appendix K.
Appendix K Prompt Template

We provide the comprehensive prompt templates utilized throughout our framework: Table 10 details the transformation of question decompositions into declarative evidence; Table 11 defines the instruction for the reasoning policy; Table 12 and Table 13 outline the step-level faithfulness verification protocol for multihop reasoning tasks and OOD math tasks, respectively; Table 14 specifies the criteria for judging final answer correctness .
